doctrine.principleAriaLabel: Principle {id} of the Fórmula do Dota de Corrida

1.title: It's NEVER the other player's fault
1.body: The responsibility is always yours, 100% of the time. Blaming others is the number one source of conflict inside a match. The moment you stop looking at others and start looking at yourself, you begin to see where you can improve through honest self-criticism.

2.title: Frustration is born from unmet expectations
2.body: Expecting teammates to pick the heroes you'd want, wanting them to make plays the way you would, counting on a specific call for help that never comes — all of it breeds frustration, because you're projecting an outcome that doesn't depend on you alone. Training yourself to place no expectations on others strengthens your emotional intelligence during matches.

3.title: Cognitive parallax
3.body: Every player reads the game differently, according to their own perspective. There is no absolute truth in any single play: what looks right to you may make no sense to your teammate in that moment. The more you accept this reality, the fewer internal and external conflicts arise — and the better you perform.

4.title: Making mistakes is part of learning
4.body: Don't fear your mistakes — they're the first step toward improvement, as long as you own them and learn from them.

5.title: Either you win, or you learn
5.body: There will be matches where, no matter what you do, the loss is inevitable. But that can't — and shouldn't — break your consistency. Every defeat must be seen as a point of growth. Losing is part of it. Improving is a choice.

6.title: It's not arrogance, it's responsibility
6.body: 99.5% of players don't know how to play Dota 2. You've become superior to the other 9 players in your match — superior in knowledge, in emotional control, in your ability to adapt. Knowing more means that now it's you who carries the win.

7.title: Net worth (gold) over time is the real KPI
7.body: Frags/KDA don't define your performance — they're just a consequence. The true performance indicator is the amount of net worth (gold) accumulated or extracted from the map relative to time. That's why the clock must be your primary guide for every decision.

8.title: Measurable goals (500 GPM)
8.body: As a Core: 5,000 gold by minute 10, 10,000 by minute 20. As a Support: half of that — 2,500 by minute 10 and 5,000 by minute 20. These numbers equal 500 GPM (gold per minute), the minimum acceptable for anyone who wants to extract the most from the resources available on the map.

9.title: Playing Core is easier
9.body: The more net worth you accumulate in less time, the simpler your decisions become. With more resources, you get access to better items, greater impact in fights, and the ability to dictate the pace of the match.

10.title: Mid is the best lane to grow
10.body: You share experience with no one. It's possible to hit 1 level per minute — the level race. If you haven't reached Immortal yet, play Mid until you've at least hit Divine. It's the fastest, most efficient path to developing your overall sense of Dota 2.

11.title: Solo Mid OR a full stack of 5
11.body: Only two setups work: 100% solo Mid (with chat muted in the social settings) or a full party of 5. Any other combination stalls your growth, because it mixes coordination with isolation.

12.title: Smurfs offer a challenge
12.body: The presence of smurfs changes neither your MMR nor your growth process. A smurf offers a challenge — after all, you can only improve by facing people better than you. Even if you lose 99% of your matches against smurfs, always see the upside: either you win, or you learn.

13.title: 70% win rate → +1000 MMR over 100 matches
13.body: At a 70% win rate, 100 matches give you 70 wins and 30 losses. A net surplus of 40 wins × 25 MMR = +1000 MMR. Playing 5 matches a day, you complete the 100 matches in 20 days — and climb 1000 MMR. The secret is staying consistent and following the method.

14.title: Guardian → Divine in 2 months
14.body: Guardian sits between 800 and 1800 MMR; Divine starts at 4600. Holding a 70% win rate, it takes around 300 matches — playing 5 a day, roughly 2 months. With method and discipline, months of frustration turn into real, tangible progress.

1.title: Blame Culture
1.ex0: Always blaming others for your own mistakes — "mid diff", "pos 5 bot", "noob carry".
1.ex1: The "I played well, the team is just bad" mindset.
1.ex2: Inability to take responsibility for your own decisions.

2.title: Giving Up Early (Give Up Mentality)
2.ex0: By minute 10-15 they're already typing "gg go next" in chat.
2.ex1: They refuse to fight or to try and turn the match around.
2.ex2: They write off the match over small mistakes or early disadvantages.

3.title: Forcing Unsuitable Strategies (Stubborn Playstyle)
3.ex0: Insisting on off-meta tactics or heroes without mastering them.
3.ex1: Failure to adapt to what the match demands.

4.title: Lack of Communication or Toxic Communication
4.ex0: Completely ignoring chat and pings, or using them only to flame.
4.ex1: Chat/voice spammers who insult and get in the team's way.

5.title: Rage Quit / Disguised AFK
5.ex0: After dying a few times, they go farm jungle without interacting with the team.
5.ex1: They leave the keyboard and wait for the match to end.

6.title: Intentional Feeding (Griefing)
6.ex0: Out of wounded ego or a tantrum, they start dying on purpose.
6.ex1: Mindset: "if you won't do what I want, I'll feed until this ends."
6.directSeverityNote: Feeding in a match with a coach goes STRAIGHT to a 14-day suspension.

7.title: Inflated Ego
7.ex0: "I deserve to be in Ancient/Divine, but my team holds me down here."
7.ex1: They use this as a justification for toxic behavior.

8.title: Fights Over Role and Lane
8.ex0: Fighting over a lane or role that's already taken (2 mids, 3 carries).
8.ex1: Mindset: "if it's not my way, it won't be anyone's way."

9.title: Disrespecting Leadership (Anti-team)
9.ex0: Refusing to listen to calls or follow the team's plays.
9.ex2: Refusing to accept suggestions, even polite ones.

10.title: Prejudice, Xenophobia and Racism
10.ex0: Offensive comments about nationalities, accents, and playstyles.
10.ex1: Examples: "Brazilians only know how to feed", "Russians are all trolls", "laggy Peruvian".
10.ex2: They contribute to a toxic, disrespectful environment.
10.directSeverityNote: Immediate ban. No warning, no second chance.

11.title: Hero Simulator
11.ex0: Knows how to use the hero's abilities but plays with no game objectives (the clock, net worth, runes, the experience altar).
11.ex1: Reacts to the opponent's plays instead of extracting net worth in the shortest time possible.
11.ex2: Valve itself has admitted it: 99.5% of players don't know how to play Dota 2 — they play on autopilot.

12.title: Placing Expectations on Others
12.ex0: Expecting a pull from the support, a gank from mid, specific help from a teammate that never comes.
12.ex1: Distinct from "frustration is born from expectations" (the mental principle) — this is the ACTIVE BEHAVIOR of projecting outcomes onto others.
12.ex2: You can (and should) place expectations on yourself. On other people, never.

13.title: Systemic Victimhood
13.ex0: Building a chronic victim identity: "matchmaking is out to get me", "the bad luck is always on my side", "Dota is unfair to me".
13.ex1: Distinct from Blame Culture (#1) — it's not a one-off reaction to a match, it's a recurring pattern.
13.ex2: Every time you lose and pin it on others, you build a shield against your own growth.

14.title: Refusing the Post-Loss Audit
14.ex0: An anti-pattern of OMISSION: failing to ask the pivot question after every loss.
14.ex1: The canonical question: "what could I have done differently to win this match, even with the team playing badly?"
14.ex2: Without the audit there's no learning — and without learning, a loss stops being a step up and becomes a cycle.

15.title: Seeking Fun in a Space of Competition
15.ex0: Joining FORMULADOTA looking for fun violates the cultural contract.
15.ex1: This isn't a place to have fun — it's a place to learn, grow, and compete.
15.ex2: Competition isn't tied to fun. If you want fun, play Turbo or Unranked.

manifesto.metaTitle: Why FormulaDota — it's not you, it's the system
manifesto.metaDescription: Dota 2's official competitive environment has three structural flaws: anonymity, a closed top, and a fragmented ranking. FormulaDota builds the environment that's missing — real identity, seasons that reset, and a single ranking.
manifesto.heroSubtitle: Dota is one of the best games in the world. What's broken is Valve's competitive environment — and even the legends are leaving.
manifesto.grubbyQuote: “I love Dota 2. But this may be the end.”
manifesto.grubbyBody: An esports legend — multiple-time Warcraft III world champion and a benchmark for positive mindset. When the most level-headed player in the scene — the very one who teaches you to keep your head right — is driven out by toxicity, it's proof: it's not the player, it's the system with no rules.
manifesto.comparisonIntro: Valve's official matchmaking has three structural flaws. They're not bugs — they're design choices that produce the environment that drives away anyone who takes the game seriously. FormulaDota doesn't try to fix Valve: it builds the environment Valve should have.

anonimato.problemBody: With no real identity, toxicity carries no consequence. Flaming, smurfing, dodging punishment — all of it faceless, with no reputation, no cost. The anonymous have nothing to lose.
anonimato.solutionBody: 1 person, 1 identity — public, unique, with reputation attached. Anonymity is forbidden. Those who act badly answer for it, by name. Those who play right build a history.

topo.problemBody: Without a true reset, MMR inflates and the top stays forever in the hands of those who've hoarded it for years. No matter how much you improve — the door to the top closed before you ever arrived.
topo.solutionBody: Every cycle starts over. The top is reconquered each season, not inherited. A committed player — even starting today — has a real path to #1.

regiao.problemBody: The ranking is fragmented by region. Isolated communities, with no common axis, no single race that counts for everyone. “Top of the Americas” never meets “top of Europe.”
regiao.solutionBody: One race, with no regional borders. A common axis for everyone who plays under the same doctrine — where #1 truly means #1.

metodologia.metaTitle: Methodology — The Fórmula do Dota de Corrida
metodologia.metaDescription: The theory behind the Formula: why Dota is a race, why net worth over time is the universal KPI, and why the methodology works beyond the game.
metodologia.heroSubtitle: Why Dota is a race. Why net worth over time is the universal KPI. Why the methodology works beyond the game.
metodologia.thesisStatement: “Dota 2 isn't about killing heroes. It's about <red>progressing your own hero</red> consistently and denying your opponent's consistent progression.”
metodologia.s1Intro: The line above is the whole document. Everything that follows is the proof that it's true.
metodologia.s1Body: It's not opinion. It's not a playstyle. It's not preference. It's what the game literally is — by the design it was given by its creators, by the mathematical rules that govern its system, and by the logic of everything that happens within it. Those who understand this manipulate outcomes. Those who don't think matchmaking is out to get them.
metodologia.s1Note: “Allow yourself to question. Everything and anything. That is what truly grows a person. FORMULADOTA is a place for those who seek real evolution.”
metodologia.s2Intro: What decides the outcome of a match isn't individual talent, hero choice, or kill count — it's the speed at which you accumulate net worth relative to time.
metodologia.s2Quote: “Dota 2, just like a Formula 1 race, is about speed and efficiency — but not the speed you're thinking of. Here, speed is measured by your ability to accumulate net worth over the course of the match.”
metodologia.s2Body: The clock is the judge of the match. Not the kill feed, not the chat, not your support's hunch. The clock. Every minute that passes without you extracting resources from the map is a minute your opponent used to extract theirs.
metodologia.s3Intro: The game's name is the argument: defend the Ancient. Not stack up kills.
metodologia.s3Body: Before Dota 2 existed as Valve's standalone game, the concept was born in 2003 as a Warcraft III custom map: DotA — Defense of the Ancients. The original creators (Eul, then Guinsoo, then IceFrog) named the game after its very soul: defending the Ancient.
metodologia.s3Li0: The match's ultimate objective is to destroy the enemy Ancient, not to rack up kills
metodologia.s3Li1: To reach the enemy Ancient, you have to defend your own throughout the entire match
metodologia.s3Li2: Someone who dies 30 times but keeps the Ancient standing can win; someone who gets 30 kills and loses the Ancient always loses
metodologia.s3Close: The game was born defensive in its DNA. It was named defensive. It rewards defense.
metodologia.s4Intro: Dota is the most cognitively complex game humanity has ever designed — the last to fall to artificial intelligence.
metodologia.s4Quote: “Dota 2 is the chess of the future. And chess was fundamental to the development of artificial intelligence. Man, chess is really hard. DOTA 2 is harder than chess, because DOTA 2 is the chess of the future.”
metodologia.s4Body: The proof is practical: OpenAI spent years developing neural networks capable of beating professional Dota players — the first AI win over a pro team came in 2019. Chess was solved in 1997. Go in 2016. Dota was the last to fall.
metodologia.s4Close: Dota has emergent patterns. Beneath the infinite variables lie patterns that repeat — water runes, bounty/effect runes, altars, the Tormentor, power spikes. Those who recognize the patterns manipulate outcomes. Those who don't play on autopilot and think they're just unlucky.
metodologia.billionsStatement: There are more than <red>8 billion</red> people on the planet, and <red>99.99%</red> are terrible at Dota 2. The difference between them and the top has never been talent — it's <red>method</red>.
metodologia.s5Title: Net Worth Over Time Is the Universal KPI
metodologia.s5Intro: In May 2026, public OpenDota data records 8,109,737 ranked players worldwide. The distribution proves where the opportunity lies.
metodologia.s5Body1: 56% of the world's players sit in Guardian + Crusader + Archon — 4.5 million people stuck in the same place. That's the audience the Formula was designed for.
metodologia.s5Body2: The difference between Archon and Divine isn't talent. It isn't having more time. It's knowing and applying the methodology.
metodologia.s5ShowcaseCaption: The top of the ranking — where the Formula aims to take you.
metodologia.s6Intro: Most matches are decided by players waiting for the opponent's mistake, not by creating spectacular plays.
metodologia.s6BlockTitle: The other player's mistake is free information.
metodologia.s6Quote: “You have to learn the art of playing on your opponent's mistake. You don't need to make flashy plays.”
metodologia.s6Body: Defending costs less energy than attacking. The opponent's mistakes are free information — you spend no energy causing them. They happen because the opponent doesn't have the methodology.
metodologia.s6Layer0: Mechanical (aggro) — pulling creep aggro to win the trade in lane
metodologia.s6Layer1: Informational — forcing the opponent to read the match incorrectly
metodologia.s6Layer2: Psychological — punishing the opponent mentally so they make the mistake you need
metodologia.s6Close: The Formula also recognizes that first blood matters — if you take down an enemy before the fight even starts, the rest of it is 5v4. But the first blood that counts is the one you land, not the one you attempt.
metodologia.s7Intro: A 70% win rate isn't motivation — it's arithmetic anyone can verify.
metodologia.s7PathLabel: Applied to the Guardian → Divine path:
metodologia.s7Close: These numbers are the mathematical consequence of commitment. What most players lack isn't ability — it's consistency.
metodologia.s7ShowcaseCaption: Match after match — that's how consistency turns into MMR.
metodologia.s8Intro: Valve once stated: “99.5% of Dota 2 players don't know how to play Dota 2.” The Formula calls those 99.5% hero simulators.
metodologia.s8BlockTitle: Knows everything about the hero. Nothing about the game.
metodologia.s8Lead: The hero simulator is the player who:
metodologia.s8Li0: Knows how to use the hero's abilities
metodologia.s8Li2: Knows how to build popular items
metodologia.s8Li3: But plays with no map objectives — the clock, net worth, runes, altars, the Tormentor, Roshan
metodologia.s8Close: 99.5% of players do exactly this. The Formula is the leap from that 99.5% to the 0.5% who understand the game. And once you see it, you can't unsee it.
metodologia.s9Title: The Expansion of Your Perception of Reality
metodologia.s9Intro: Everything laid out so far seems to be about Dota. It isn't only about Dota.
metodologia.s9Body: Joining the Formula is an invitation to expand your perception of reality. The method that makes you a better player is the same method that makes you a better professional, a better partner, a better steward of your own life.
metodologia.s9Li0: Allowing yourself to question — the founding act. Without questioning, there's no pattern recognition, no refinement of method, no honest self-criticism.
metodologia.s9Li1: Pursuing self-responsibility — in Dota, “it's never the other player's fault.” In life, it means you stop blaming failures on the company, the government, your family, or chance.
metodologia.s9Li2: Practicing placing no expectations on others — calibrating expectations only on yourself frees up mental energy to build.
metodologia.s9Li3: Recognizing patterns in complex systems — seeing that markets, relationships, and career growth also have recognizable patterns.
metodologia.s9Li4: Discipline over motivation — consistency and method produce predictable results in any area.
metodologia.s9Li5: Defending more than attacking — a life principle of strategic patience that applies to negotiations, conflicts, and career decisions.
metodologia.s9Close: The person who breaks out of the hero simulator in Dota is the same one who breaks out of the life simulator in every other area. The Formula is the method. Dota 2 is the laboratory.
metodologia.s10Intro: Dota 2 isn't a game of luck disguised as skill. It's a game with verifiable mathematical logic.
metodologia.s10Body1: Those who recognize the logic manipulate outcomes. Those who don't blame it all on bad matchmaking luck.
metodologia.s10Body2: FORMULADOTA isn't a place for those who just want to climb medals. It's a place for those who seek real evolution — starting with Dota, ending with their entire life.
metodologia.s10Note: “The point here isn't to entertain you — it's to change you from the inside, in the way you think, play, and react to Dota.”
metodologia.s10Attribution: — Pedro Paulo, author of the methodology

Q1_1.prompt: You lose a match and you're convinced the problem was your pos 5 who fed bot lane the whole game. What does the Fórmula tell you to do?
Q1_1.a: Report the ally and move on to the next game without thinking about it any further.
Q1_1.b: Take responsibility yourself, 100% of the time, and look for where you could have done better.
Q1_1.c: Note down the ally's name to avoid him in the future.
Q1_1.d: Accept that some matches are the team's fault and that's fine.
Q1_1.rationale: The responsibility is always yours, 100% of the time — blaming others is the main source of conflict.

Q1_2.prompt: Why does blaming others stall your evolution?
Q1_2.a: Because the report system punishes those who complain too much.
Q1_2.b: Because while you're looking at others, you don't look at yourself and you fail to see where you can improve through self-criticism.
Q1_2.c: Because allies notice it and play worse on purpose.
Q1_2.d: Because it lowers your GPM in the next match.
Q1_2.rationale: Stopping looking at others and looking at yourself is what unlocks self-criticism.

Q1_3.prompt: Which phrase sums up the First Rule of the Fórmula do Dota de Corrida?
Q1_3.c: It's NEVER the other person's fault.
Q1_3.d: Mute the chat and play solo.

Q2_1.b: An expectation you projected onto an outcome that didn't depend on you alone.
Q2_1.c: Matchmaking put you with a weak team.
Q2_1.d: A lack of voice communication on the team.
Q2_1.rationale: Frustration is born from unmet expectations — you project an outcome that doesn't depend on you alone.

Q2_2.prompt: How does the Fórmula tell you to train emotional intelligence within matches?
Q2_2.a: By taking a deep breath before every teamfight.
Q2_2.b: By recognizing when you're creating expectations of others and training the habit of not getting attached to them.
Q2_2.d: By avoiding playing when you're tired.
Q2_2.rationale: The exercise is to recognize the expectation and not get attached to it — this strengthens emotional intelligence.

Q2_3.prompt: Which of these is a direct example of an unmet expectation cited in the doctrine?
Q2_3.a: Expecting the server to have no lag.
Q2_3.b: Expecting allies to pick the heroes you'd want them to.
Q2_3.c: Expecting to win every match of the day.
Q2_3.d: Expecting the enemy to miss an ability.
Q2_3.rationale: Expecting allies to pick certain heroes, make plays your way, or give help that never comes.

Q3_1.prompt: Your ally makes a play that to you is clearly wrong, but he seemed confident. What does cognitive parallax explain about this?
Q3_1.a: That he was trolling on purpose.
Q3_1.b: That each player interprets the game through their own perspective — what looks right to you may not make sense to him in that moment.
Q3_1.c: That he has lower MMR than you.
Q3_1.d: That you should take command of the team.
Q3_1.rationale: Cognitive parallax — there is no absolute truth in any given play; each person interprets it through their own perspective.

Q3_2.prompt: Accepting cognitive parallax produces what practical effect in your match?
Q3_2.b: Fewer internal and external conflicts, and better performance.
Q3_2.c: It makes allies agree with you.
Q3_2.d: It reduces the number of enemy smurfs.
Q3_2.rationale: The more you accept this reality, the fewer conflicts arise and the better your performance.

Q3_3.prompt: Which statement is aligned with cognitive parallax?
Q3_3.a: There is an absolutely correct play in every situation and everyone should see it.
Q3_3.b: There is no absolute truth in any given play — it depends on each person's perspective.
Q3_3.c: Whoever has more MMR is always right in their read.
Q3_3.d: The correct read is that of the player with the best KDA.
Q3_3.rationale: There is no absolute truth in any given play.

QL5_2.a: 200 XP, enough for level 2 on its own.
QL5_2.b: 240 XP (3 melee creeps at 57 + 1 ranged at 69), which is exactly what's needed to go from level 1 to level 2.
QL5_2.c: 180 XP, half of what's needed for level 2.
QL5_2.rationale: Each wave = 3 melee (57 XP) + 1 ranged (69 XP) = 240 XP, exactly what's needed for level 2.

QL5_3.prompt: Two players sharing the lane XP (with 1 deny) reach level 2 on the death of which creep, and why?
QL5_3.a: On the 8th creep, because 8 creeps add up to 240 split between two.
QL5_3.b: On the 9th creep — the first creep of the third wave — because the creep XP is odd and the "half" of XP is taxed by Valve, since hero XP is a whole number.
QL5_3.c: On the 6th creep, because XP doubles in a dual lane.
QL5_3.d: On the 12th creep, because splitting always delays level 2.
QL5_3.rationale: With 1 deny, level 2 comes on the death of the 9th creep (1st creep of the 3rd wave); the odd XP has its "half" taxed by Valve.

QL5_4.prompt: In an unfavorable matchup, why is it still worth focusing on hitting level 2 first?
QL5_4.a: Because the opponent gives up when he loses the XP.
QL5_4.b: Because the duo that hits level 2 first will always be stronger than the duo still at level 1, regardless of the matchup — 4 skills carry a far bigger power spike than 2 skills.
QL5_4.c: Because level 2 guarantees the first tower.
QL5_4.d: Because the matchup has no influence at all on the early game.
QL5_4.rationale: Whoever hits level 2 first is always stronger than whoever is at level 1; 4 skills > 2 skills in power spike.

QL5_5.prompt: You're in the first 3 waves of a normal lane. What does the Fórmula tell you to do with the wave?
QL5_5.a: Cut the wave to pressure the tower early.
QL5_5.b: Pull immediately to speed up the farm.
QL5_5.c: Just play the lane — no pull and no cutting the wave; focus attentively and intentionally on the first 9 creeps and nothing else. Pull only after winning the lane.
QL5_5.rationale: Focus on the first 9 creeps; no pull and no cutting the wave. Pull only after winning the lane.

QL6_1.prompt: Why does the Fórmula treat the first 3 waves as the highest-return investment of the match?
QL6_1.a: Because that's when you get the most gold per creep.
QL6_1.b: Because Dota 2 applies the butterfly effect very aggressively: a good start (the first 3 waves) makes the mid and late game tend to be good as well.
QL6_1.c: Because after 3 waves the lane is over.
QL6_1.d: Because it's the only moment when you can farm.
QL6_1.rationale: The butterfly effect is aggressive in Dota 2; a good start amplifies and makes the rest consistent.

QL6_2.prompt: A player botches the early game badly and thinks he "can still recover comfortably in the late game." Why does this contradict the doctrine?
QL6_2.a: Because the late game doesn't exist in the Fórmula.
QL6_2.b: Because early mistakes propagate through the butterfly effect — that's why L4 and L5 are so decisive: they're the input that amplifies across the rest of the match.
QL6_2.c: Because recovering in the late game is forbidden.
QL6_2.d: Because the opponent always wins the late game.
QL6_2.rationale: Early mistakes propagate; L4 and L5 are the input of the butterfly effect.
